text.p: Following is a chronology of the sale of Creditanstalt-Bankverein, Austria's longest running privatisation since World War Two.
1990 - The ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party agreed to put the state's 70 percent of Creditanstalt ordinary voting shares up for sale.
March 14, 1991 - Parliament stipulated the sale must safeguard Austrian interests.
April 30, 1993 - Austrian co-operative banking group Raiffeisen targeted a merger with Creditanstalt.
May 6, 1993 - Finance Minister Ferdinand Lacina turned down Raiffeisen after Creditanstalt's board opposed the plan.
Jan, 1994 - Switzerland's CS Holding emerged as a potential buyer.
March 16, 1994 - Austrian industrialists, including juice maker Rauch and carton board maker Mayr-Melnhof, began forming the "Austrian consortium". Insurer EA-Generali said it was keen to join.
May 6, 1994 - Savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse Bank (First Austrian) joined the group, which received open support from Creditanstalt executives.
May 19, 1994 - CS Holding said it wanted to buy 20-30 percent of Creditanstalt shares at once, then take full control.
May 26, 1994 - The Austrian consortium, led by EA-Generali, offered 7.2 billion schillings for 37 percent of voting shares.
Aug 16, 1994 - Creditanstalt employees threatened mass resignations if the CS Holding bid succeeded.
Sept 12, 1994 - CS Holding, citing disillusionment with political in-fighting, dropped its bid.
Jan 19, 1995 - Germany's Allianz Holding AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG submitted an offer for Creditanstalt.
March 14, 1995 - The Austrian consortium placed a fresh bid of 10 billion schillings for half the government's stake and proposed selling the rest through a secondary offering.
March 16, 1995 - Allianz and Bayerische Hypo withdrew, citing an unfair due-diligence process.
April 6, 1995 - Ferdinand Lacina resigned as finance minister, replaced by little-known accountant Andreas Staribacher.
July 14, 1995 - J.P. Morgan, hired as the government's adviser, valued the bank stake at 18 billion schillings, including a premium of six billion schillings for majority control.
Sept 7, 1995 - Austria invited new bids by October 9.
October 1995 - The coalition government collapsed and a new election was called, putting the Creditanstalt sale on ice.
Dec 18, 1995 - The Social Democrats again emerged as the strongest party in the vote.
Jan 2, 1996 - Staribacher resigned and was replaced by Transport Minister Viktor Klima.
June, 1996 - First Austrian proposed a holding company to control it and Creditanstalt, Creditanstalt executives reject the plan.
July 17, 1996 - Klima said the consortium must make a bid by the end of August or he would reopen the race.
Sept 2, 1996 - Klima extended the deadline to September 6.

Sept 6, 1996 - First Austrian announced it had quit the consortium. The rest of the group, led by EA-Generali bid nine billion schillings for half the government's stake and proposed selling the remainder through a secondary offering.
Sept 23, 1996 - Klima rejected the group's bid because it was not for the entire stake, invited new bids by November 15.
Nov 13, 1996 - Die Erste rejoined the Austrian consortium led by EA-Generali, which confirmed it would make a new offer.
Nov 15, 1996 - The deadline for indicative offers expired.
Nov 20, 1996 - Media reports said the Austrian consortium had bid 720 to 730 schillings a share for two-thirds of the state's stake. Klima said he received two indicative offers.
Dec 11, 1996 - Market leader Bank Austria supervisory board voted to make an offer, but gave no details.
Dec 13, 1996 - Austrian parliament called on the government to reject Bank Austria's offer.
Dec 16, 1996 - Klima confirmed Bank Austria and EA-Generali led group's bids and a third bid by entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek.
Dec 27, 1996 - Finance ministry reopened tender to allow existing three bidders to improve their offers and set a new deadline on January 10.
Jan 8, 1997 - EA-Generali group raised its bid but gave no details.
Jan 9, 1997 - The coalition government agreed to convene for an emergency meeting of leaders on January 11 to discuss the political impasse surrounding the sale.
Jan 10, 1997 - The deadline for the final tender expired at 0800 GMT. Klima said he expected to make a decision on the sale before a special session of parliament on January 14.
Minutes before deadline ended, Bank Austria raised its bid but revealed no details.
Jan 11, 1997 - The government coalition partners held an emergency meeting on the sale of the bank.
Jan 12, 1997 - After 11 hours of deliberation with coalition partners, Klima announced they had reached a deal whereby Creditanstalt would be sold to Bank Austria for 17.161 billion schillings.
As part of the deal Creditanstalt would remain independent for at least five years after its sale and Bank Austria would be taken out of public control step by step.
Bank Austria said the merger would double earnings per share over the next five years and that it would finance the acquisition with its own resources.
